lines.text: The cheetah is the fastest animal on land. So why does it so often slow down, in the middle of a chase?
In Botswana, scientists fitted five wild cheetahs with collars carrying GPS and motion sensors. They recorded three hundred and sixty-seven runs.
The fastest reached fifty-eight miles an hour. But most hunts were run at far more moderate speeds.
Because a chase isn't won on the straight. It's won in the turns.
At full speed, no animal can turn sharply. So when an impala swerves, the cheetah brakes. Hard. In a later study, the hunters could brake about seventy percent harder than the animals they chased.
Brake. Turn with the prey. Then accelerate out of the turn.
And the old belief that cheetahs give up because they overheat? Another team measured it. Body temperature stayed steady through the chase. It rose afterwards.
Even with all that skill, only about one run in four ended in a meal.
The fastest animal on Earth doesn't win by running flat out. It wins by knowing when to slow down.
